promptText: What is the core architectural change that let Transformers solve both the long-range dependency problem and the training-parallelism problem that RNNs/LSTMs struggled with?
options: Replacing recurrence entirely with self-attention, so every position can directly attend to every other position in a single parallel computation with no step-by-step relay of hidden state
Adding more gates to the recurrent cell so information decays more slowly across timesteps
Increasing the hidden state's dimensionality so more history can be compressed into one vector
Processing the sequence in both forward and backward directions simultaneously, like a bidirectional RNN
explanation: Self-attention lets token 500 attend directly to token 1 in one step with no intermediate relay, and because no position recurrently depends on another position's output at the same layer, every position can be computed simultaneously on parallel hardware.

promptText: Why do Transformers need an explicit positional encoding added to token embeddings before self-attention runs?
options: Raw self-attention is permutation-invariant — it computes pairwise Query/Key matches with no inherent notion of which token came first, so 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' would otherwise produce identical pairwise interactions
Positional encoding is required so that the softmax function can be computed correctly
Without positional encoding, the Query and Key vectors would have mismatched dimensions
Positional encoding replaces the need for a feed-forward sublayer in each Transformer block
explanation: Self-attention on its own treats a sequence as an unordered bag of tokens; positional encoding injects order information explicitly so the otherwise order-blind mechanism can represent which token occurred where.

promptText: What is the key architectural difference between an encoder-only model like BERT and a decoder-only model like GPT?
options: BERT uses bidirectional attention where every token can see every other token, suiting understanding tasks; GPT uses masked (causal) attention where a token can only see itself and earlier tokens, suiting autoregressive generation
BERT has no attention mechanism at all, relying purely on feed-forward layers, while GPT uses self-attention exclusively
BERT can only process a single token at a time, while GPT processes the entire sequence in one step
BERT and GPT are functionally identical; the only difference is the training dataset used
explanation: Bidirectional attention fits tasks where the full input is available upfront (classification, embeddings), while causal masking is required to match the real constraint of generation, where future tokens genuinely do not exist yet at inference time.

promptText: What does a causal mask do inside a decoder's self-attention, and why is it necessary during training?
options: It sets attention scores for any future position to effectively negative infinity before softmax, so a token can never attend to positions after it — this keeps training consistent with the fact that future tokens don't exist yet at real inference time
It randomly zeroes out attention weights to regularize the model against overfitting
It reduces the dimensionality of the Query and Key vectors to speed up computation
It ensures every token receives exactly equal attention weight regardless of content
explanation: If training allowed a token to peek at future tokens while predicting the current one, the model would learn to rely on information unavailable at actual generation time, making trained behavior inconsistent with deployed behavior.

promptText: What does an inference server's KV cache store, and why does it exist?
options: The Key and Value vectors computed for every previous token, at every layer, cached because those vectors never change once computed — avoiding the wasted work of recomputing them from scratch on every new generated token
A cache of the model's entire weight matrices, duplicated per active user session
A cache of previously generated full responses, used to skip generation entirely for repeated prompts
The Query vectors for every future token the model expects to generate next
explanation: Since every future token's attention computation needs the Key/Value vectors of every past token, and those vectors are fixed once computed, caching them trades memory for avoiding redundant recomputation at every decoding step.

promptText: Why are residual (skip) connections wrapped around each sublayer in a Transformer block?
options: They give gradients a direct additive path backward through the network that bypasses the sublayer's own transformation, making it practical to stack dozens (or over a hundred) of blocks without the training signal degrading
They reduce the total number of parameters needed in the feed-forward sublayer
They replace the need for positional encoding by preserving token order implicitly
They allow the model to skip processing tokens that are deemed irrelevant by the attention mechanism
explanation: A residual connection adds a sublayer's input directly to its output, so backpropagated gradients have an unobstructed shortcut path, addressing the same class of gradient-degradation concern that motivated gating in LSTMs, but through architecture instead.

promptText: Why is self-attention's cost described as quadratic in sequence length, and what is the direct practical consequence?
options: Computing Q·Kᵗ requires comparing every token's Query against every other token's Key, producing an n×n score matrix, so both compute and memory grow proportionally to n² — meaning doubling input length roughly quadruples prefill cost, which is why context window size is a hard, headline cost constraint
Quadratic cost comes from running the feed-forward sublayer twice per token to stabilize training
Quadratic cost only applies to the softmax computation, not to the underlying matrix multiplications, so it can be avoided entirely by skipping softmax
Quadratic cost is a property of positional encoding, not of the attention computation itself
explanation: The n×n pairwise score matrix is a direct, unavoidable consequence of the 'every token attends to every other token' design goal, which is exactly why retrieval-based approaches exist instead of simply stuffing an entire long document into the prompt.

promptText: What is the structural difference between Pre-LN and Post-LN Transformer blocks, and why has Pre-LN become the default for large-scale training?
options: Post-LN normalizes after the residual addition, repeatedly resetting the residual stream's scale based on immature early-training sublayer outputs, which risks instability without careful learning-rate warmup; Pre-LN normalizes the sublayer's input before transformation, leaving the residual path itself untouched by normalization and giving much more stable, predictable gradient flow through very deep stacks
Post-LN applies normalization only to the feed-forward sublayer, while Pre-LN applies it only to the attention sublayer
Pre-LN removes the need for residual connections entirely, while Post-LN requires them
Post-LN is used exclusively in encoder-only models, while Pre-LN is used exclusively in decoder-only models
explanation: Because Pre-LN keeps an unimpeded identity path from input to output, it tolerates more aggressive learning rates and less delicate warmup at scale, which is why it became close to the default as model depth scaled into the hundreds of layers, even though well-tuned Post-LN can sometimes reach a marginally better final loss.

promptText: How does Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) differ from both standard multi-head attention (MHA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA), and why did models like Llama adopt it?
options: GQA splits query heads into groups where each group shares one Key/Value head, sitting between MHA (every head has its own K/V, g=h) and MQA (all heads share one K/V, g=1) — it was adopted because full MHA's KV cache cost was too high for long-context serving, while plain MQA's quality cost was judged too steep, so GQA recovers most of MHA's quality while keeping most of MQA's memory savings
GQA eliminates the Query projection entirely, relying only on Key and Value vectors for attention
GQA is identical to MQA but adds an extra feed-forward layer after each attention head
GQA increases KV cache memory relative to MHA in exchange for improved attention quality
explanation: KV cache size is proportional to the number of distinct K/V heads stored; GQA's grouping gives an explicit, tunable knob between MHA's full quality/full memory cost and MQA's minimal memory/reduced quality, which is why it became the default for large open-weight decoder-only models.

promptText: FlashAttention is often described as a pure engineering win with no accuracy trade-off. What does it actually change, and why does that change speed things up?
options: It computes the exact same mathematical result as standard scaled dot-product attention but restructures the computation (via tiling and online softmax) so the full n×n score matrix is never fully written to slow GPU memory (HBM) — since standard attention is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth, not raw arithmetic, avoiding that memory traffic is what produces the speedup
It approximates the softmax function with a cheaper polynomial, trading a small amount of accuracy for significant speed
It reduces sequence length by discarding tokens the model predicts are least relevant before computing attention
It replaces the Query/Key/Value projections with a single shared projection matrix to cut compute in half
explanation: Modern GPU arithmetic throughput has outpaced memory bandwidth, so an operation that writes and reads a large matrix to HBM becomes bandwidth-bound; FlashAttention avoids materializing that matrix at all while producing an identical numerical result.

promptText: Sliding-window attention restricts each token to attend only within a fixed-size local neighborhood. How can a model built entirely from such local-attention layers still capture dependencies between tokens far outside any single window?
options: Stacking multiple sliding-window layers lets information propagate transitively: a token's representation, already carrying influence from its own window in one layer, falls within the next token's window in the following layer, so information can relay across many layers to reach tokens far beyond any single layer's window — similar to how stacked convolutional layers build a large effective receptive field
Sliding-window attention secretly computes full quadratic attention internally and only reports a restricted subset of scores to the user
Each window is dynamically resized during inference to always cover the full sequence when a long-range dependency is detected
Long-range dependencies are simply lost entirely and cannot be recovered by any architectural means
explanation: Depth substitutes for per-layer range: information takes multiple hops (and passes through intervening nonlinearities) to travel far, rather than reaching its destination in one direct attention step, trading some fidelity and directness for linear-in-length cost per layer.

promptText: Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) rotate Query and Key vectors by an angle proportional to token position. What key mathematical property makes this an effective way to encode position?
options: Because rotation matrices compose, the dot product between a Query rotated by position m and a Key rotated by position n depends only on the relative offset (m − n), not on their absolute positions — so relative position information falls out of the attention score computation itself
Rotating the vectors guarantees the attention score matrix becomes symmetric, which simplifies the softmax computation
The rotation angle is learned during training for every possible pair of positions, similar to a lookup table
Rotating Query and Key vectors eliminates the need for the softmax function entirely
explanation: The rotation-composition identity means q'_m · k'_n reduces to a function of (n−m) alone, injecting relative-position sensitivity directly into the attention score via pure geometry rather than by adding a position vector to the input embedding beforehand.

promptText: The feed-forward sublayer costs O(n·d²) per layer while the attention sublayer costs O(n²·d), where n is sequence length and d is model width. At what relationship between n and d does attention's cost overtake the feed-forward sublayer's cost as the dominant compute driver?
options: Roughly when n ≈ d — for typical chat-length prompts against models with d in the thousands, feed-forward sublayers actually dominate total compute, and attention only becomes the dominant cost once sequence length grows well past model width, which is why attention-efficiency techniques matter disproportionately for long-context serving rather than short-prompt workloads
Attention always dominates total cost regardless of n and d, since it is quadratic while the feed-forward cost is only linear in n
Feed-forward cost always dominates regardless of n and d, since d² grows faster than n² for any practical model size
The two costs are equal only when n and d are both exactly zero, making the comparison meaningless in practice
explanation: Setting n·d² ≈ n²·d and simplifying gives the crossover at n ≈ d; this is the concrete numeric justification for why FlashAttention and sparse/windowed attention matter far more for long-context serving than for short, chat-sized prompts.

promptText: Given the RoPE rotation identity q'_m · k'_n = qᵗ·R((n−m)θ)·k, why does this specifically solve a limitation that plain sinusoidal or learned absolute positional encodings have?
options: Absolute encodings are added to the token embedding before attention runs, so the model must learn to infer relative relationships indirectly from two absolute position signals; RoPE instead makes the relative offset fall directly out of the attention score computation itself, meaning every pair of tokens with the same relative distance produces the identical rotational relationship regardless of where in the sequence that pair occurs
RoPE removes the need for a Value vector, since position alone determines the attention output
RoPE guarantees the model can extrapolate perfectly to any sequence length without any further scaling technique
RoPE makes attention computation exactly linear in sequence length instead of quadratic
explanation: Because the rotated dot product depends only on (n−m), the same learned relative pattern applies consistently no matter where a pair of tokens sits in the sequence — a property absolute encodings don't provide directly, though RoPE alone still requires additional scaling techniques (NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) to extrapolate well beyond its trained length.

promptText: Kernel-approximated linear attention (e.g., Performer, Linformer) offers an asymptotically better cost than exact softmax attention, yet top-tier production LLMs have largely stuck with exact quadratic attention plus complementary optimizations (FlashAttention, GQA, sliding windows). Why?
options: Linear-attention approximations have generally underperformed exact softmax attention on language-modeling quality at comparable scale, especially on tasks requiring sharp retrieval of one specific fact from far back in context — behavior that softmax's ability to concentrate weight on a few highly relevant tokens supports well but that low-rank or kernel approximations tend to smear out
Linear attention is mathematically incompatible with the causal masking required for autoregressive generation
Linear attention requires more GPU memory than exact quadratic attention at every sequence length
Linear attention cannot be combined with positional encoding of any kind
explanation: The exactness of softmax attention appears to matter disproportionately for the specific 'needle in a haystack' precision properties that evaluations and users reward, which is why production systems have favored exact-but-optimized attention (hardware-efficient kernels, KV-cache reduction) over approximate linear attention despite its attractive asymptotic complexity.
